newsitem.title: USA: Fidelity manager sees more bond fund consolidation.
newsitem.headline: Fidelity manager sees more bond fund consolidation.

text.p: The Fidelity Investments fixed income division will continue to consolidate its 61 bond funds in 1997 as it seeks more consistent returns, the division's managing director Fred Henning, Jr., said on Monday.
Henning said his goal is to actively manage bond portfolios using a benchmark such as improving "by 75 basis points above the Lehman Aggregate that takes in the taxable side."
Fidelity's bond funds, with some $45 billion in assets, "had too many products left over from the 'flavor of the month' phase," Henning, 55, said in a telephone interview.
"What we want to do now is take a careful look at the bonds funds and any overlapping objectives," he said.
He said his goal is to land each of the bond funds in the first or second quartile over a three-year period.
"We're looking to pick up a basis point or two, incremental returns, without losing a basis point," he said. "We want consistent return."
Henning said he expected "more mergers and consolidations" of Fidelity's bond funds to follow three such consolidations in 1996.
Fidelity, the nation's largest mutual fund company, named Henning managing director of its fixed-income unit in May after Thomas Steffanci's departure.

Henning has changed the operating climate at Fidelity's fixed-income unit. In the past, he said, the division had operated in much the same way as its equity counterpart: strong individual portfolio managers basing investment decisions on their personal judgements about the future direction of the market and interest rates.
"The portfolio fund manager basically made the decision, with the advice (of traders and analysts) if he or she wanted," he explained.
Henning said that under his direction, the manager remains the fiduciary head, but the traders, the quantitative and credit analysts all function as a team.
Henning said focus groups indicated that bond fund investors "want something that's predictable, that they can understand and that there are no surprises."

He said he believes "You can't quantify (markets') directions, or interest rates but if our decisions are well thought out and we clearly have the imput of the trading desks, the fund analysts, the credit analysts and we can quantify these things, then we can make a good judgement."
